R01-A-01: A familiar picture of the responsible thinker holds that she believes nothing on another's say-so until she has satisfied herself that the speaker is reliable. On this view, testimony is a second-class source of knowledge, legitimate only when it can be cashed out in the currency of one's own perception and reasoning: I may believe the timetable because I have found timetables accurate before, and I may believe my doctor because I have, or could obtain, evidence of her competence. The picture has the appeal of self-reliance. It seems to keep the knower in charge of what she knows. The difficulty is that almost nobody could meet its demands, and the few who tried would know very little. Consider how much of what an ordinary adult believes was simply told to her: the shape of the continents, the date of her own birth, the existence of cells, the fact that a city she has never visited lies where the maps place it. To check the reliability of these sources she would have to rely on further sources, whose reliability would in turn need checking. The independent track record the picture asks for is itself largely assembled from testimony. A child who refused to believe her teachers until she had verified their credentials would never acquire the language in which credentials are described. It does not follow that we may believe whatever we are told. The better view is that a hearer is entitled to accept what she is told unless she has some reason for doubt: a speaker with an evident motive to deceive, a claim that collides with what she already has good grounds to believe, a manner that suggests guesswork rather than knowledge. On this view the burden is reversed. Trust is the default, and it is suspicion, not acceptance, that must be earned by evidence. This is not credulity, because the default is sensitive to defeaters; the hearer who ignores a glaring sign of deceit is not exercising her entitlement but neglecting it. Defenders of the stricter picture are right about one thing. A default of trust is only as good as the hearer's alertness to the signals that should override it, and that alertness is unevenly distributed and easily exploited. The con artist's whole craft consists in suppressing the cues that would trigger doubt. But this shows that we need to cultivate sensitivity to defeaters, not that we must abandon trust as a starting point. A community in which everyone demanded proof before belief would not be more rational than ours; it would merely be poorer in what it could collectively know.
R01-A-02: The sceptic's argument has an irritating simplicity. You claim to know that you are sitting in a room reading. But if you were dreaming vividly, or if your experiences were being produced by some elaborate deception, everything would seem exactly as it now does. Since you cannot tell from the inside that you are not in such a situation, you cannot rule it out; and if you cannot rule it out, the sceptic concludes, you do not know that you are reading. The argument generalises to almost everything, and many careful attempts to refute it have the air of a lawyer winning on a technicality rather than of anyone actually seeing the truth. One response is to concede the argument and shrug: perhaps we know nothing, but we must act as if we did, and so nothing of practical importance changes. This concession is too generous. It treats the sceptic's standard, that knowing requires excluding every alternative one cannot distinguish from the actual situation, as if it were simply the correct standard, which we happen to fall short of. Yet we nowhere apply that standard outside the philosophy seminar. A birdwatcher who reports a heron on the riverbank is not asked whether she has excluded the possibility of a mechanical decoy indistinguishable at that distance; she is asked whether she looked carefully, knows her birds and had a clear view. If a park ranger has just announced that decoys have been placed along that stretch of river, the question changes, and it is right that it should. What this suggests is that the alternatives a knower must exclude are fixed by something other than bare conceivability: by what is live in the circumstances, by what a reasonable person has some ground to take seriously. The sceptic does not discover a hidden flaw in our ordinary claims; he changes the subject by importing a standard that no ordinary claim was ever meant to satisfy. This is why his argument feels at once unanswerable and beside the point. None of this makes scepticism worthless. Its exaggerated standard has the merit of exposing how much of our confidence rests on background assumptions we rarely state, and in particular circumstances, the decoy case among them, those assumptions deserve scrutiny. The error lies in moving from the observation that every assumption could in principle be questioned to the conclusion that every assumption must be questioned before anything is known. The first is a useful reminder; the second would make knowledge impossible by definition, and a definition that guarantees its own emptiness is a poor account of what we were trying to describe.
R01-A-03: When two experts disagree about a question the rest of us cannot assess, it can seem that the layperson has only two options: to become an expert herself, or to pick a side at random. Neither is attractive. The first is usually impossible within the time available, and the second makes a mockery of the idea that belief should answer to evidence. But the dilemma is false. Although the layperson cannot judge the dispute directly, she can often judge the disputants, and judgements of that kind can be reasonable even when the subject matter remains opaque to her. Several kinds of evidence are available. She can ask whether either expert has a record of predictions that can be checked, and how those predictions fared. She can ask whether one of them stands to gain from being believed, through money, reputation or loyalty to an institution. She can ask how the rest of the field divides, bearing in mind that a majority counts for more when its members reached their views independently than when they all learned them from the same teacher. None of these questions requires understanding the dispute itself. Each concerns the circumstances in which a claim is advanced rather than its technical content, and each can be answered, at least roughly, by an attentive citizen with no specialised training whatever. One tempting source of evidence is less useful than it looks. Laypeople often favour the expert who argues more fluently, answers objections more quickly and seems more at ease. Yet these are skills of performance, and they are only loosely connected with being right. A careful scientist may hedge, pause and admit uncertainties that a confident charlatan would brush aside, and an audience that rewards confidence is, in effect, rewarding the very habit that should make it suspicious. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that public debate, with its brief exchanges and its appetite for memorable phrases, is arranged almost entirely so as to display performance, and so to favour the disputant who has mastered it. It would be a mistake to conclude that the layperson's position is comfortable. Track records are often unavailable for the questions that matter most, interests can be hidden, and a field can be captured by a fashion that makes its consensus less independent than it appears. The indirect methods narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it. Still, a choice made on such grounds is not a coin toss, and treating it as one hands an advantage to whoever is most willing to exploit the public's sense of helplessness.
R01-A-04: Suppose you and a colleague whom you regard as your equal in competence and care examine the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions. Neither of you has information the other lacks; neither has reason to think the other was tired or distracted. What should you do? An influential answer holds that you should move towards your colleague's view, giving her opinion the same weight as your own. The thought behind it is simple. From a neutral standpoint, the disagreement is evidence that one of you has erred, and you have no reason, independent of the dispute itself, to think the error is hers rather than yours. To stand firm would be to treat the mere fact that a conclusion is yours as a reason to favour it. This principle seems to me correct over a wide range of cases, and it is more demanding than most people find comfortable. It condemns the familiar move of discounting a dissenter precisely because she dissents: 'she is usually so sensible, but on this question she has plainly lost her way'. If the only evidence that she has lost her way is that she disagrees with you, the reasoning simply assumes what is in question. Yet the principle cannot be applied without qualification. Imagine two equally able auditors reviewing the same short ledger, one of whom concludes that the accounts balance while the other reports that the firm's assets exceed the number of grains of sand on the earth. The first auditor need not split the difference. Her confidence that her colleague has blundered does not rest on her own conclusion about the ledger; it rests on the absurdity of his, which she can recognise without relying on the reasoning they disagree about. What licenses holding firm, then, is not that a view is one's own but that one has grounds, independent of the dispute, for locating the error on the other side. The equal-weight principle survives, but it turns out to be a claim about what to do when such independent grounds are absent, not a rule that applies whatever one knows. Critics sometimes press a further objection: since thoughtful people disagree about the equal-weight principle itself, the principle seems to require its own defenders to lose confidence in it. This is less damaging than it first appears. A principle about how to respond to disagreement may well recommend reduced confidence in itself without thereby becoming false; it would show only that the matter is genuinely hard, which no one denied. What the objection does reveal is that conciliation cannot be the whole story about rational belief. A thinker who revised every view the moment a peer dissented would soon have no settled views left to revise, and some account is still owed of what entitles anyone to a starting point.
R01-A-05: We tend to assume that each of us has a special and nearly infallible access to our own minds. Others must infer what I think and feel from my speech and behaviour, whereas I, it seems, am acquainted with my own mental states directly, without any need for inference or interpretation. For some states the assumption is plausible. If I sincerely report a sharp pain in my knee, it is hard to see what better evidence anyone could have, including me, about whether the pain is there. But the assumption is usually extended, without much reflection, to a quite different class of facts: the facts about why I did what I did. Here the case for special access is far weaker. Imagine a shopper who chooses one of several identical scarves laid out in a row and who, asked why, cites the richer colour or the finer weave of the one she took. Since the scarves really are identical, her explanation cannot be true, yet it is offered sincerely and without hesitation. What she supplies is not a report of a cause she observed operating within her but a plausible reconstruction, drawn from a shared and largely unexamined theory of human motivation, of the kind anyone might give of why a person would choose a scarf. An onlooker armed with the same commonsense theory could have produced the same explanation, and would have been no more and no less likely to be right. It is tempting to conclude from such cases that self-knowledge is an illusion and that we stand to ourselves essentially as strangers do, but that conclusion overreaches. The shopper's error concerns the causes of a past choice, and about such causes she may well be no better placed than anyone else. But there is another kind of question about which her position is not that of an observer at all. If she is asked which scarf she will wear tomorrow, or whether she thinks scarves make a sensible gift, she does not answer by studying evidence about herself; she answers by deciding, or by considering the merits of scarves. Her authority here derives from the fact that the answer is, in part, up to her. The lesson, then, is not that the first person has no privilege but that its privilege has been misplaced. We are poorly placed to discover, by looking inward, the forces that moved us; we are well placed to settle what we will stand by. Confusing the two invites a double error: an unearned confidence about our own motives, and an exaggerated scepticism that would deny us even the authority we exercise whenever we make up our minds.
R01-A-06: 'I did not know' is among the oldest excuses there is, and often among the best. We do not blame a pharmacist who dispenses a medicine that was contaminated at the factory in a way no inspection could detect, nor a traveller who carries a parcel for a friend without any reason to suspect what it contains. In such cases ignorance breaks the link between what a person did and what she intended, and blame that disregarded this would be blame for bad luck. But the excuse has a counterfeit form. Consider a manager who tells his staff that he wants results and does not want to hear how they are achieved. When it later emerges that the results were achieved by falsifying safety records, he can say, truthfully, that he did not know. Yet his not knowing was not something that happened to him; it was something he arranged. He foresaw that there might be facts he would be obliged to act on, and he took steps to ensure that he would never be in possession of them. To accept his excuse would be to reward precisely the foresight that makes him responsible. The distinction, then, is not between knowing and not knowing but between ignorance a person suffers and ignorance a person cultivates. The cultivated kind does not cancel responsibility; if anything, it adds a second fault to the first, since the person has both allowed a wrong to occur and taken care to shield himself from ever having to confront it. This is why such a person can seem, on reflection, no better and perhaps rather worse than someone who knew the facts plainly and still did nothing about them. One should not push this too far. No one can investigate everything, and a demand that we trace the full history of every product we buy and every institution we deal with would be impossible to meet and would make ordinary life unworkable. Routine purchases, everyday dealings with banks and employers, and the countless small transactions of daily life proceed, quite properly, on the assumption that things are roughly as they appear. The charge of cultivated ignorance is fair only where a person had some particular reason to suspect a problem and chose not to look because looking might oblige him to act. Without such a reason, not inquiring is simply the normal condition of finite beings, and it is no more blameworthy than failing to read every book in a library.
R01-A-07: Intellectual humility is praised more often than it is defined, and the praise tends to blur it with other things. Sometimes it is equated with low confidence, as if the humble thinker were one who held every opinion loosely. Sometimes it is identified with deference, the willingness to yield to those who know more. And sometimes it means no more than a modest manner, the habit of prefacing one's claims with 'I may be wrong, but'. Each of these captures something, yet none of them can be the virtue itself, because each can be present where humility is absent and absent where humility is present. Take low confidence first. A person may be unsure of everything out of sheer timidity, believing too little rather than too much, and timidity of this kind is no more admirable than arrogance; it is merely a different way of misjudging one's evidence. Conversely, someone may be entirely certain that the earth orbits the sun, and rightly so, without any failure of humility. Deference fares no better. It is often wise, but a thinker who deferred to every apparent authority would be credulous rather than humble, and one who refused to defer to a genuine expert on a question outside her competence might be guilty of several faults without its being clear that humility is the one she lacks. As for the modest manner, it concerns how one presents oneself to others, and it can coexist with a private conviction that one is never mistaken. The phrase 'I may be wrong' is cheap to say. A more promising account locates humility in a person's relation to her own limitations. The humble thinker is one who notices the gaps in her knowledge, the places where her reasoning is shaky and the biases to which she is prone, and who takes these into account: she seeks out the evidence she lacks, rechecks the steps she is unsure of, and discounts the conclusions she has special reason to want. This is compatible with great confidence where her grounds are good. Indeed, it is partly because she is alert to where her grounds are poor that her confidence elsewhere deserves to be taken seriously. Her humility, on this view, is not a feeling about herself but a settled pattern of attention and correction, visible chiefly in what she does whenever her own judgement is at stake. It may be objected that this account makes humility indistinguishable from good reasoning in general. Anyone who reasons well, after all, attends to the strength of her evidence. But the two can come apart. A scientist may be superb at weighing evidence about the world and yet curiously blind to the ways in which her own ambitions shape which questions she asks and which results she finds convincing. Her failure is not a failure to reason about stars or cells; it is a failure to treat herself as one more possible source of error. That reflexive attention, directed at the reasoner rather than at the subject matter, is what the word humility usefully picks out. The account has a further merit: it explains why humility can be overdone. A person preoccupied with her own limitations, forever cataloguing the ways in which she might be mistaken, may become unable to act on what she knows or to contribute what she has to offer. Owning one's limitations includes keeping them in proportion, and the thinker who is paralysed by self-scrutiny has misjudged them as surely as the one who ignores them.
R01-A-08: It is natural to think of understanding as knowledge in a higher concentration. On this view, a person who understands why bridges stand or why prices rise simply knows more than one who does not: more facts, and in particular more facts about causes. Understanding would then be knowledge of a special subject matter, the reasons why, but it would be knowledge all the same, answerable to the same standards and vulnerable to the same defeats. The view has difficulty with a familiar figure, the student who has memorised the correct explanation. Asked why the seasons change, she replies, accurately, that the earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit, so that each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for part of the year. She has the answer from a reliable textbook and a reliable teacher, and by most accounts of knowledge she knows why the seasons change. Yet ask her what would happen if the tilt were greater, or why the seasons are reversed between the hemispheres, and she is at a loss. She possesses the explanation as a sentence rather than as something she can use. What she lacks is not a further fact but a grasp of how the facts she already has depend on one another, the ability to follow the explanation into cases for which it was not stated. If this is right, understanding is less a matter of what one has been told than of what one can do with it, and this has a surprising consequence. Knowledge is usually held to require truth: one cannot know what is false. Understanding seems more forgiving. Much of what we rightly call scientific understanding is achieved through models that are, taken literally, false. The simple model of a gas treats its molecules as points that occupy no space and exert no forces on one another except in collision, which no actual molecule does; yet a student who has mastered that model understands a great deal about why gases behave as they do, and understands it partly because the model leaves out complications that would obscure the pattern. It would be odd to say that her understanding is defective merely because the model is false, and odder still to say that someone who had memorised a more accurate description, but could do nothing with it, understood more. This should not be taken to mean that understanding floats free of truth altogether. An idealisation earns its place only when its departures from reality are irrelevant to the questions it is used to answer; the point-particle model serves well for gases at ordinary densities and misleads at very high ones, and part of understanding the model is knowing where it stops working. A story that got the dependencies wrong, however fluently it could be manipulated, would yield not understanding but a skilful illusion of it. The claim, then, is not that falsehood is harmless but that the relation between understanding and truth is looser and more selective than the relation between knowledge and truth: understanding demands accuracy in the respects that bear on the dependencies grasped, and tolerates distortion elsewhere. The distinction matters beyond philosophy. Educational systems that measure success by the reproduction of correct statements will reward the memorising student and may never detect what she is missing, since what she is missing shows itself only when the question changes. Testing for understanding requires, at least in part, asking questions the student has not been prepared for.
